notes: Hosea is short (14 chapters) and organized around one sustained device — the prophet's own marriage as a living parable of the LORD's covenant with Israel — rather than a large cast. Tiering reflects that: two person-tier managers (Hosea, Gomer), three sign-named children as submanagers under Hosea (they were named by direct divine command, not by their parents), and five law/theme tiers covering the book's other major named/recurring content (Baal worship, calf worship, Israel's recalled sinful history, the 'mercy not sacrifice' teaching, and the closing call to return). Historical allusions to earlier-book figures (Jacob, the unnamed 'prophet' of 12:13 traditionally understood as Moses, the Gibeah atrocity, Baal-peor) are cited as verses/funFacts within the 'Israel's Sinful History Recalled' law tier rather than given new standalone character entries, since these figures take no independent action within Hosea itself — only Jacob is explicitly named there, and his mentions are historical recollection, not narrative participation. Naming collisions flagged: the prophet 'Hosea' shares its underlying Hebrew name with 'Hoshea,' the last king of Israel (2 Kings 17:1), and with 'Oshea,' Joshua's original name (Numbers 13:16) — three different KJV spellings of the same name for three different people. 'Jeroboam' in the 1:1 superscription is Jeroboam II son of Joash, not Jeroboam I son of Nebat (founder of the calf worship condemned later in the book) — flagged explicitly since only the name, not the distinguishing patronymic, would otherwise make this ambiguous. Hosea 6:6 ('For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings') — flagged as missing in the prior draft — is now cited under the dedicated 'Mercy, Not Sacrifice' law tier, with its double quotation by Jesus (Matthew 9:13; 12:7) noted.

characters.name: Hosea

genealogy.note: Identified only as 'the son of Beeri' (1:1); no mother is named. The superscription dates his ministry to the reigns of Judah's kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and Israel's king Jeroboam — Jeroboam the son of Joash (Jeroboam II), not to be confused with the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat, founder of the calf worship Hosea condemns at 8:5-6 and 10:5.

funFacts: His name means 'salvation,' sharing its root with the names Joshua and Jesus.

KJV spells the prophet's name 'Hosea,' but the last king of Israel bears the same underlying Hebrew name spelled 'Hoshea' (2 Kings 17:1), and Joshua's original name is rendered 'Oshea' at Numbers 13:16 before his renaming — three distinct KJV spellings of one Hebrew name for three different people, not to be confused with one another.
The only Old Testament prophet whose own marriage is used as a sustained, multi-chapter living parable of God's relationship to Israel.
characters.perkNote: Represents steadfast covenant love that buys back an unfaithful spouse rather than abandoning her.

verses.note: Superscription: 'the word of the LORD that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri' — dates his ministry by the kings of Judah and Israel.
Commanded to 'take unto thee a wife of whoredoms' — the LORD's command that begins the sign-marriage; he takes Gomer.
Commanded a second time to love an adulterous woman; buys her back 'for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley.'
Tells her she must dwell with him many days without playing the harlot — a picture of Israel's coming discipline before restoration.

characters.name: Gomer

genealogy.note: Called 'a wife of whoredoms... a daughter of Diblaim' (1:3). The unnamed woman Hosea is later commanded to love in 3:1 ('a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress') is traditionally identified with Gomer, but chapter 3 does not name her again — the text itself does not explicitly confirm the identification.

funFacts: Bears three children whose divinely-given names function as prophetic sign-acts against Israel.
In chapter 2 the LORD addresses 'your mother' (Israel personified through Gomer) as having credited Baal for grain, wine, and oil that were actually gifts from the LORD (2:5, 8).
characters.perkNote: Represents Israel redeemed at a set price rather than cast off — echoes a discounted buy-back.

verses.note: 'So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.'
Pursues 'lovers,' crediting them for bread, water, wool, flax, oil, and drink.
'she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil' — the LORD, not Baal, was the true source.
Restoration oracle: the LORD betroths Israel to himself forever 'in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness.'

characters.name: Jezreel

genealogy.note: Firstborn son; named directly by the LORD's command, not chosen by his parents (1:4).

funFacts: Name means 'God sows' or 'God scatters'; also the name of the valley/city where Jehu massacred the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9-10) and where Ahab seized Naboth's vineyard.
His name's meaning is reversed from judgment to hope by the book's end — 'great shall be the day of Jezreel' (1:11) and 'I will sow her unto me in the earth' (2:22-23, wordplay on 'Jezreel').
characters.perkNote: A judgment-name repurposed into a promise of replanting and increase.

verses.note: 'Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.'
'great shall be the day of Jezreel' — his name reused as a title of future restoration.
'they shall hear Jezreel. And I will sow her unto me in the earth.'

characters.name: Lo-ruhamah

genealogy.note: Daughter; named 'Lo-ruhamah' ('not pitied' / 'not having obtained mercy') by direct divine command (1:6).

funFacts: Her name is reversed in the restoration oracle — 'I will call her Ruhamah' ('having obtained mercy'), Hosea 2:1, 23.
Marks the point where God declares He will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel specifically (1:6), while the house of Judah is shown mercy at the same time (1:7).
characters.perkNote: A withheld-mercy name later restored — 'Ruhamah,' mercy obtained.

verses.note: 'Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel.'
By contrast, the LORD says He 'will have mercy upon the house of Judah' at this time.
'Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah' — the reversal.
'I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy.'

characters.name: Lo-ammi

genealogy.note: Second son; named 'Lo-ammi' ('not my people') by direct divine command (1:9).

funFacts: His name is reversed to 'Ammi' ('my people') in the restoration oracle (2:1, 23).

Hosea 1:10 immediately pairs the harsh naming with a promise that Israel's numbers will be 'as the sand of the sea' and they will be called 'the sons of the living God' — quoted by Paul in Romans 9:25-26.
characters.perkNote: A covenant-broken name restored to full sonship.

verses.note: 'Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.'
'ye are the sons of the living God' promised in the same breath as the judgment-name.
'I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people.'

characters.name: Baal Worship
characters.purpose: Frames Israel's idolatry as marital infidelity — Israel credits Baal for the grain, wine, oil, wool, and flax the LORD actually provided (2:5, 8), pursues Baal under shady trees on the hills (4:13), and must be stripped bare and led back into the wilderness to be won again (2:9-15). (Attribution: Adopted by Israel from Canaanite Baal-religion; condemned throughout Hosea's oracles as the LORD's rival for Israel's devotion.)
funFacts: The Hebrew word 'baal' also simply means 'husband/lord' — part of the book's wordplay: the LORD promises Israel will call Him 'Ishi' (my husband) rather than 'Baali' (my Baal/lord), Hosea 2:16-17.
The LORD vows to 'take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, that they be no more remembered by their name' (2:17).
characters.perkNote: Exposing false credit given to Baal for the harvest undercuts the idols' apparent value.

verses.note: Israel did not know the LORD gave the corn, wine, and oil later 'prepared for Baal.'
'the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them' — judged.
Restoration: Israel will call the LORD 'Ishi' (my husband), no longer 'Baali'; Baal's names removed from her mouth.
Sacrifices offered 'upon the tops of the mountains... under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good.'
Recalls Israel joining themselves to 'Baal-peor' in the wilderness and becoming 'abominable like the thing they loved.'
'they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images.'
'when he offended in Baal, he died' — Ephraim's fall tied directly to Baal worship.

characters.name: Calf Worship
characters.purpose: Condemns Israel's self-manufactured golden-calf worship at Bethel/Dan as illegitimate idolatry distinct from Baal worship — a homegrown substitute for the LORD, doomed to be smashed to pieces and carried off as tribute to Assyria. (Attribution: Man-made: 'the workman made it; therefore it is not God' (8:6). Hosea does not name the calves' original royal sponsor, though 1 Kings 12:28-29 credits Jeroboam I's shrines at Bethel and Dan.)
funFacts: Hosea mockingly renames Bethel ('house of God') as Beth-aven ('house of iniquity/nothing') at 4:15 and 10:5 because of the calf shrine there.
10:6 pictures the calf-idol itself carried off to Assyria as tribute — the object of worship becomes a captive.
characters.perkNote: The calves are exposed as 'not God' — manmade objects worth less than claimed.

verses.note: 'thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off... the workman made it; therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.'
'The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Beth-aven.'
The calf-idol itself 'shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb.'
'they have made them molten images of their silver... they say... Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves.'

characters.name: Israel's Sinful History Recalled
characters.purpose: Argues that Israel's present unfaithfulness continues a long pattern of rebellion — reaching back to the patriarch Jacob, the days at Gibeah, the sin at Baal-peor, and the Exodus from Egypt itself — and of foolish alliance-seeking with foreign powers instead of trust in the LORD. (Attribution: Hosea, recounting Israel's own national history as a prophetic indictment.)
funFacts: Hosea 12:3-4 recalls Jacob taking 'his brother by the heel in the womb' (cf. Genesis 25:26) and having 'power with God... over the angel, and prevailed' (cf. Genesis 32:24-28), and 12:12 recalls Jacob fleeing to Syria and serving for a wife (cf. Genesis 28-29) — historical allusions to earlier Genesis events, not new action within Hosea itself.
Hosea 11:1 ('When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt') is quoted by Matthew (2:15) of the infant Jesus' return from Egypt.
Hosea 7:11 compares Ephraim to 'a silly dove without heart' flitting between Egypt and Assyria for help instead of the LORD.
characters.perkNote: Recounting the LORD's past faithfulness despite Israel's repeated failures underscores His enduring covenant loyalty.

verses.note: 'they like men have transgressed the covenant' (KJV wording; some translations render 'like Adam') — a broken covenant recalled.
'Ephraim is a cake not turned' — half-baked, ruined by foreign entanglement.
Ephraim 'like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.'
'they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah' (cf. Judges 19-20).
Israel's sin at 'Baal-peor' in the wilderness (cf. Numbers 25).
'O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah' repeated.
'I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.'
Recalls Jacob at his birth and his striving with the angel.
Recalls Jacob fleeing to Syria and serving for a wife.
'by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet was he preserved' — the prophet is not named in the text (traditionally understood as Moses).

characters.name: Mercy, Not Sacrifice
characters.purpose: Declares that steadfast covenant love ('mercy'/lovingkindness) and relational knowledge of God matter more to the LORD than ritual sacrifice — one of the book's central theological statements, and among the most quoted verses in the Minor Prophets. (Attribution: Spoken by the LORD through Hosea.)
funFacts: Quoted twice by Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew — 9:13 and 12:7 — both times against Pharisees who prioritized ritual over compassion.
Sits just after the LORD's complaint that 'your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away' (6:4), immediately before His own explanation of what He truly desires (6:6).
characters.perkNote: Prioritizes relationship and steadfast love over transactional ritual.

verses.note: 'there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land.'
'my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge... because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee.'
'For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.' Quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.

characters.name: Call to Return
characters.purpose: Invites Israel to abandon idols and return to the LORD in genuine repentance, promising healing, free love, and flourishing restoration — the book's closing resolution to the marriage/harlotry metaphor developed throughout. (Attribution: Hosea's closing prophetic exhortation to Israel.)
funFacts: 14:2 instructs Israel to 'take with you words' rather than animal sacrifices when returning to the LORD, offering 'the calves of our lips' (praise) instead.
14:8 has the LORD say 'I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found' — a closing image reversing the false 'green tree' idolatry condemned at 4:13.
characters.perkNote: Repentance is met with free, healing love rather than continued anger (14:4).

verses.note: 'Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us.'
'O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God... take with you words, and turn to the LORD.'
'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.'
'I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.'
Closing wisdom saying: 'the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them.'
